# First steps in R

Even without any data loaded, we can use R like a calculator. If we type `2 + 2` and "Run Code" (in R Studio: `Ctrl / CMD + Enter`), it calculates the answer:

```{r add-solution}
2 + 2
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where do I type this?

Look for the "Console" in RStudio. By default it's in the pane on the bottom left. You can move it, by going to `View > Panes > Console on Right`.
:::

## Getting started using R

Some other mathematical operators you probably recognize are: 

- `-` (for subtraction or negative numbers), 
- `*` (multiplication), 
- `/` (division), and 
- `^` (power, as in $3^2$ = `3^2`). 

There are also functions for 

- square root (`sqrt()`),
- rounding to say 1 digit (`round(..., digits = 1)`), 
- logarithm (`log()`, or base 10, `log10()`), 
- exponential (`exp()`).

Combining these operators, along with some parentheses, allows us to calculate many things. For example, calculate BMI (body mass index) for a person who is 180cm tall and weighs 85 kg.

```{r calc}
85 / (1.8^2)
```

We can also save these height and weight values with an arrow, `<-`, and use them later for the calculation.

```{r calcletter}
wt <- 85
ht <- 180
wt / ((ht / 100) ^2)
```

But what if we had height and weight for, say 3 people?

- Person 1: weight 85, height 180
- Person 2: weight 90, height 190
- Person 3: weight 95, height 200

It would be annoying, not to mention error-prone, to have to calculate each BMI separately. To save all 3 heights or weights at once, we use a vector, by putting all 3 values inside `c()`, separated by commas: `c(85, 90, 95)`. 
```{r vector}
wt <- c(85, 91, 95)
ht <- c(180, 190, 200)
wt / ((ht / 100)^2)
```

Now that we're working with more than one observation, we might also need functions like:

- mean (`mean()`),
- standard deviation (`sd()`),
- median (`median()`), 
- sum (`sum()`), or
- minimum and maximum (`min()`, `max()`).

```{r mean-median}
wt <- c(85, 90, 95)
ht <- c(180, 190, 200)
bmi <- wt / ((ht / 100)^2)
mean(bmi)
```

Combining this information in a dataset, and then performing the calculation is more efficient. We'll talk more about that in the next two sections.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```


```{r showdataset}
mydata <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3),
                 wt = c(85, 90, 95),
                 ht = c(180, 190, 200)) |> 
  mutate(bmi = wt / ((ht / 100)^2))
mydata
```

## Some R basics

R is a case sensitive programming language. The saved objects `n` and `N`, for example are not the same! On the same note, typing `Mean()` will not get you the `mean()` function.

```{r}
n <- 30
N <- 100
n / N
```

You cannot use a `,` the middle of an object's [name](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-basics.html#sec-whats-in-a-name), however `_` (underscore) is fine. Try to make names you do not mind typing out.

```{r}
#| eval: false
one_name
anotherName
and.another.name
```


You may see `#` in R code (pound symbol, hash mark). This is generally used to [comment](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-basics.html#comments) whole or partial lines. It can also be used to comment out

```{r}
# this is a commment
2 + 2 # this is also a comment
# 3 + 3 this whole line is commented out and does not run
```

## Finding help with R

There are a lot of functions to keep track of that you might want to use. How do you find them? 

- In the bottom right, there's usually a "help" pane. You can try searching there for what you need. This is often the best way to find a function and figure out how to use it.
- If you start typing the beginning of a function in the "console", it probably tries to autocomplete it for you. For example, typing `mean` in the console brings up a list of functions starting with the letters `mean`.
- The help menu in RStudio has various useful links, including to "cheat sheets".
- A web or AI search usually does a pretty good job of finding code in `tidyverse` packages or, say, in `gtsummary`. That's because these packages have all their documentation in a package website, including "articles", such as a [`tbl_summary()` tutorial](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/articles/tbl_summary.html).
